title: Leaf Detectives: Parent Guide
endLine: Sort leaves by steady shapes and edges, not seasonal color.

scenes.tts: Which leaf clues would you trust in summer and fall? In thirty minutes, you can help your child sort fallen leaves and test which clues hold up.
scenes.caption: Which leaf clues would you trust in summer and fall? In thirty minutes, you can help your child sort fallen leaves and test which clues hold up.
scenes.visual: Spread a small fan of schematic fallen leaves of different shapes and colors on the cream tabletop. Slide one into an empty hoop as the opening question is spoken.
scenes.narration: Which leaf clues would you trust in summer and fall? In thirty minutes, you can help your child sort fallen leaves and test which clues hold up.

scenes.visual: Title card on the same warm cream tabletop with subtle leaf silhouettes drifting slowly at the margins. Large bold dark text reads: Leaf Detectives — Parent Guide.

scenes.tts: Your child practices looking closely and sorting by one rule at a time. They also practice asking a question and checking it. Instead of memorizing tree names, they discover which leaf clues stay steady all year.
scenes.caption: Your child practices looking closely and sorting by one rule at a time. They also practice asking a question and checking it. Instead of memorizing tree names, they discover which leaf clues stay steady all year.
scenes.visual: On the tabletop, three schematic leaves sit beneath three clean animated icons that transform softly in place: a magnifying outline tracing leaf veins, two sorting hoops pulsing gently, and a simple summer-to-fall sun-and-leaf dial turning slowly.
scenes.narration: Your child practices looking closely and sorting by one rule at a time. They also practice asking a question and checking it. Instead of memorizing tree names, they discover which leaf clues stay steady all year.

scenes.tts: Grab a bag or basket, two hoops or string loops, thin paper, and a peeled crayon. Take a ten to fifteen minute walk to collect eight to twelve different fallen leaves. Printed leaf photos work if you stay indoors.
scenes.caption: Grab a bag or basket, two hoops or string loops, thin paper, and a peeled crayon. Take a ten to fifteen minute walk to collect eight to twelve different fallen leaves. Printed leaf photos work if you stay indoors.
scenes.visual: Friendly schematic drawings slide smoothly onto the tabletop from the left: a woven collecting basket, two string loops opening into circles, a stack of thin white paper, and a peeled crayon rolling to a gentle stop beside a fan of eight varied leaf cutouts.
scenes.narration: Grab a bag or basket, two hoops or string loops, thin paper, and a peeled crayon. Take a ten to fifteen minute walk to collect eight to twelve different fallen leaves. Printed leaf photos work if you stay indoors.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child outdoors and keep them in sight. Keep them within arm’s reach near roads, parking lots, and water. Collect only fallen leaves where permitted. Leave unfamiliar leaves and leaves with three leaflets on the ground. Even dead or fallen poison ivy can cause a rash. Never taste any plant part or mushroom. Wash hands after collecting. Keep crayon pieces and small finds away from children under four.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child outdoors and keep them in sight. Keep them within arm’s reach near roads, parking lots, and water. Collect only fallen leaves where permitted. Keep crayon pieces and small finds away from children under four.
scenes.visual: On the cream tabletop, show a schematic fallen leaf beside a path. Cross out the three-leaflet silhouette. Show an adult hand pointing out an unfamiliar leaf and leaving it on the ground, then cut to soapy hands. Finish with an adult moving crayon pieces and small leaves out of reach.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child outdoors and keep them in sight. Keep them within arm’s reach near roads, parking lots, and water. Collect only fallen leaves where permitted. Leave unfamiliar leaves and leaves with three leaflets on the ground. Even dead or fallen poison ivy can cause a rash. Never taste any plant part or mushroom. Wash hands after collecting. Keep crayon pieces and small finds away from children under four.

scenes.tts: Spread out the leaves you checked. Look at their edges, veins, and tips. Keep spiny leaves for the adult to handle. Let your child sort the leaves into two piles. Then ask, "What was your rule?" Write down their words.
scenes.caption: Spread out the leaves you checked. Look at their edges, veins, and tips. Keep spiny leaves for the adult to handle. Let your child sort the leaves into two piles. Then ask, "What was your rule?" Write down their words.
scenes.visual: The checked leaves spread across the tabletop. A pointer traces an edge, a vein, and a tip. An adult hand moves a spiny example aside. The remaining leaves glide into two groups in the string loops.
scenes.narration: Spread out the leaves you checked. Look at their edges, veins, and tips. Keep spiny leaves for the adult to handle. Let your child sort the leaves into two piles. Then ask, "What was your rule?" Write down their words.

scenes.tts: Next, sort by one feature at a time using the two hoops. Try one leaf together first: needle or flat, smooth edge or toothed, lobes or no lobes. Before each round, ask, "Which hoop do you think will hold more?"
scenes.caption: Next, sort by one feature at a time using the two hoops. Try one leaf together first: needle or flat, smooth edge or toothed, lobes or no lobes. Before each round, ask, "Which hoop do you think will hold more?"
scenes.visual: A pine needle bundle glides first into the left hoop labeled Needle while a flat oak leaf moves into Flat. The hoop labels morph smoothly to Smooth and Toothed, then Lobes and No lobes, as leaves gently glide across and a bold prompt reads: Which hoop will hold more?
scenes.narration: Next, sort by one feature at a time using the two hoops. Try one leaf together first: needle or flat, smooth edge or toothed, lobes or no lobes. Before each round, ask, "Which hoop do you think will hold more?"

scenes.tts: A bright red leaf makes color tempting as a sorting rule. Imagine using that same rule again in summer. Would leaves from the same tree land in the same pile?
scenes.caption: A bright red leaf makes color tempting as a sorting rule. Imagine using that same rule again in summer. Would leaves from the same tree land in the same pile?
scenes.visual: The hoops fade as a schematic red maple leaf moves to the center of the cream tabletop. Place an empty hoop beside it with a question mark. Keep the leaf red while the narrator asks for the prediction.
scenes.narration: A bright red leaf makes color tempting as a sorting rule. Imagine using that same rule again in summer. Would leaves from the same tree land in the same pile?

scenes.visual: Hold the red maple leaf and the empty hoop for the full thinking pause. Show the question Same pile in summer? on screen. Leave the hoop empty until the reveal.

scenes.tts: A red maple leaf can be green in summer. In fall, it can be red, orange, or yellow. Ask your child, "What color was this leaf back in July?" If you can find two differently colored leaves from the same tree, compare their shapes and edges.
scenes.caption: A red maple leaf can be green in summer. In fall, it can be red, orange, or yellow. Ask your child, "What color was this leaf back in July?" If you can find two differently colored leaves from the same tree, compare their shapes and edges.
scenes.visual: On the same tabletop, animate schematic color examples for one red maple leaf shape. Show green for summer and red, orange, and yellow as possible fall colors. Then place a green example and a red example side by side and trace their matching outlines.
scenes.narration: A red maple leaf can be green in summer. In fall, it can be red, orange, or yellow. Ask your child, "What color was this leaf back in July?" If you can find two differently colored leaves from the same tree, compare their shapes and edges.

scenes.tts: Slide a leaf under thin paper with the veins facing up. Rub with the side of a peeled crayon. The veins and edges show up. For older children, try a yes-or-no key together. Ask whether the leaf is a needle. If it is, the example key leads to pine.
scenes.caption: Slide a leaf under thin paper with the veins facing up. Rub with the side of a peeled crayon. The veins and edges show up. For older children, try a yes-or-no key together. Ask whether the leaf is a needle. If it is, the example key leads to pine.
scenes.visual: On the cream tabletop, show a leaf vein side up before sliding thin paper over it. Rub with the side of the peeled crayon until the veins and edges appear. Pull back to a pine needle and show one branch from Needle? through Yes to Pine.
scenes.narration: Slide a leaf under thin paper with the veins facing up. Rub with the side of a peeled crayon. The veins and edges show up. For older children, try a yes-or-no key together. Ask whether the leaf is a needle. If it is, the example key leads to pine.

scenes.tts: A key only covers the leaves you built it for. Help your child write questions for your own set. Give someone a leaf from that set and ask them to try the key. Rewrite any question that trips them up. Your child practices choosing clues that stay steady.
scenes.caption: A key only covers the leaves you built it for. Help your child write questions for your own set. Give someone a leaf from that set and ask them to try the key. Rewrite any question that trips them up. Your child practices choosing clues that stay steady.
scenes.visual: Keep the needle branch on the tabletop. Set down the family’s chosen leaves beside a sheet where an adult and child add questions. Show a second person following arrows for one leaf, then circle the question they paused at and erase the circle as the question is revised.
scenes.narration: A key only covers the leaves you built it for. Help your child write questions for your own set. Give someone a leaf from that set and ask them to try the key. Rewrite any question that trips them up. Your child practices choosing clues that stay steady.
